one_liner: Lean Rust Apache Arrow implementation with enum-dispatched typed arrays; about 1.7x faster than arrow-rs on a 1,000-element sum microbenchmark.
what_it_does: Minarrow is a from-scratch Rust implementation of the Apache Arrow columnar memory layout: typed IntegerArray, FloatArray, StringArray, BooleanArray, CategoricalArray and DatetimeArray, wrapped in Array and Table (RecordBatch) enums, with chunked SuperArray/SuperTable, zero-copy views and optional NdArray/Matrix types. It is not API-compatible with arrow-rs, so you convert at the boundary with to_apache_arrow()/to_polars() or the Arrow C Data Interface, and the companion minarrow-pyo3 crate moves tables to and from PyArrow through PyCapsule. It ships containers and a small set of arithmetic, bitmask and string kernels rather than a query engine, and it does not implement List or Struct types.
how_it_is_fast: Type dispatch goes through nested enums (Array -> NumericArray -> Arc<IntegerArray<T>>) instead of arrow-rs's Arc<dyn Array> plus as_any().downcast_ref, so the compiler can inline the match and hand back a concrete typed array. Every owned buffer is a Vec64 (the author's 64-byte-aligned Vec, built on the nightly allocator_api), so values are read as a plain aligned slice and fed to std::simd (portable_simd) kernels whose lane counts build.rs fixes from the target's features (SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512 or NEON). There is no new algorithm, and in the published benchmark part of the gap comes from the access pattern: the Minarrow paths iterate a slice, while the arrow-rs paths call the bounds-asserting value(i) once per element.
when_to_use: Rust code that keeps Arrow-layout columns in memory and wants typed access (arr.num().i64()) without dyn Array downcasting, especially in latency-sensitive loops over primitive i64/f64 columns.

Rust-to-Python handoff of tables to PyArrow/Polars through PyCapsule or the C Data Interface. Export is zero-copy, and the README reports 165 ns Rust->Python and 2.5 us Python->Rust for 1M rows x 2 columns. Import is zero-copy only for 64-byte-aligned buffers.
Projects that want a small dependency tree and fast builds. The base build pulls in only num-traits, vec64 and log, and the README claims compiles under 2 s.
Custom SIMD kernels that need every owned buffer guaranteed 64-byte aligned.
Passing numeric data to PyTorch, JAX or NumPy through DLPack (the ndarray and dlpack features).
when_not_to_use: You need nested Arrow types (List, Struct). They are not implemented, and Interval and Null arrays panic on C Data Interface import.
You must build on stable Rust. The crate requires nightly for allocator_api and portable_simd; CONTRIBUTING asks for 1.89.0-nightly or later, and CI runs only on nightly.

You need broad compute kernels, SQL, or Parquet/IPC file I/O in the same crate. arrow-rs plus DataFusion covers far more; Minarrow ships a small kernel set and leaves IPC streaming to the separate lightstream crate.

Your arrow-rs code already sums over values() slices or uses arrow compute kernels. The headline gap was measured against per-index value(i) calls, and the crate's own SIMD table in src/lib.rs shows Minarrow via enum at 170 ns vs arrow-rs dyn at 173 ns (parity).

You need API stability or an open contribution model. Pre-1.0 releases break often (0.17.0 switched integer division to floor semantics, 0.18.0 added enum variants), there is effectively one maintainer, and contributors must sign a CLA that assigns copyright to him.

integration.dependencies: Base: num-traits, vec64 (the author's 64-byte-aligned Vec crate) and log (a default feature). Optional, behind feature flags: arrow/arrow-schema 59.2, polars-core/polars-arrow 0.55.2, rayon, time, phf, ahash, hashbrown, parking_lot, regex, ryu, memchr and libc.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust nightly, edition 2024 (CONTRIBUTING says 1.89.0-nightly or later). Needs the allocator_api and portable_simd features.
integration.platforms: x86-64, with SIMD width picked at build time from target features (SSE2, AVX2 or AVX-512); aarch64 (NEON); wasm32 (simd128); scalar fallback elsewhere. CI runs tests on Linux, macOS and Windows but only compile-checks aarch64 and armv7 Linux. The memfd and vmap64 features are Linux-only.
integration.thread_safety: Buffer<T> is declared Send + Sync (subject to T), and arrays sit behind Arc inside the Array and NumericArray enums, so sharing them read-only across threads works. Mutating a shared buffer copies it first. Concurrent mutation is not documented, except through the lbuffer feature, which Cargo.toml marks experimental and not recommended for production.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it is not API-compatible with arrow-rs (different types and accessors). It shares the Arrow memory layout and converts to/from arrow-rs ArrayRef/RecordBatch through the C Data Interface under the cast_arrow feature, zero-copy when buffers are 64-byte aligned. It lacks List/Struct types and arrow-rs's compute, IPC and Parquet stack.

gotchas: Accessors such as Array::num() and NumericArray::i64() return a shared Arc handle only when the variant matches. Otherwise they allocate and convert (for example Int32 or Float64 to i64), and they panic on Null or a failed cast. Use the try_ variants in library code.

Zero-copy import requires 64-byte-aligned buffers. Data from pandas and Polars is typically not aligned that way, so each such column is copied into a Vec64 and a log warning is emitted (issue #57). String offsets, categorical dictionaries and Utf8View arrays are always copied on import.

build.rs bakes SIMD lane counts in from compile-time target features. The repo's .cargo/config.toml forces x86-64-v3 only for builds run inside the repository, so a downstream x86-64 build without -C target-cpu gets 128-bit SSE2 lanes.

Hot paths use unchecked access. Issue #200 (fixed in 0.18.2) showed out-of-bounds reads reachable from safe code in the string kernels and in Buffer::from_shared_column. Cargo.toml also warns that vmap64 combined with any FFI export (cast_arrow, cast_polars, memfd) is undefined behaviour.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued siblings is an in-memory Arrow array library. Pick Apache DataFusion (built on arrow-rs) when you need SQL or query execution, and Vortex or Lance when the problem is on-disk columnar encoding. Pick Minarrow when you want a lean, typed in-memory Arrow container in Rust with a fast Python handoff and can accept nightly Rust and no nested types.
verified_claims_summary: The benchmark summed 1,000 i64 values, with array construction inside the timed region, and averaged 1,000 Instant-timed runs on an Intel Core Ultra 7 155H under Ubuntu 24.04 (release build; the footnote says Rust 1.97-nightly). Minarrow IntegerArray took 88 ns (124 ns through the Array enum), against 147 ns for arrow-rs Int64Array as a struct, 181 ns through an ArrayRef downcast, and 85 ns for a raw Vec. The same five figures have been in src/lib.rs since v0.1.0 (2025-08-13, built against arrow 55.2.0), so they were probably not re-measured on the stated toolchain or against the current arrow 59.2 dependency.
status_note: Actively developed under Apache-2.0 by essentially one maintainer (0.18.2 released 2026-09-19, with frequent minor releases since v0.1.0 in August 2025); it installs from crates.io (about 7.8k downloads, 9 reverse dependencies including the author's lightstream, simd-kernels and minarrow-pyo3) but is nightly-only and pre-1.0.
